Transforming the electrical grid: the role of AI 
in advancing smart, sustainable, and secure 
energy systems
T. A. Rajaperumal1 and C. Christopher Columbus2*
Energy Informatics
Abstract
The evolution of the electrical grid from its early centralized structure to today’s 
advanced “smart grid” reflects significant technological progress. Early grids, designed 
for simple power delivery from large plants to consumers, faced challenges in 
efficiency, reliability, and scalability. Over time, the grid has transformed into a 
decentralized network driven by innovative technologies, particularly artificial 
intelligence (AI). AI has become instrumental in enhancing efficiency, security, and 
resilience by enabling real-time data analysis, predictive maintenance, demand-
response optimization, and automated fault detection, thereby improving overall 
operational efficiency. This paper examines the evolution of the electrical grid, 
tracing its transition from early limitations to the methodologies adopted in present 
smart grids for addressing those challenges. Current smart grids leverage AI to 
optimize energy management, predict faults, and seamlessly integrate electric 
vehicles (EVs), reducing transmission losses and improving performance. However, 
these advancements are not without limitations. Present grids remain vulnerable 
to cyberattacks, necessitating the adoption of more robust methodologies and 
advanced technologies for future grids. Looking forward, emerging technologies 
such as Digital Twin (DT) models, the Internet of Energy (IoE), and decentralized grid 
management are set to redefine grid architectures. These advanced technologies 
enable real-time simulations, adaptive control, and enhanced human–machine 
collaboration, supporting dynamic energy distribution and proactive risk 
management. Integrating AI with advanced energy storage, renewable resources, 
and adaptive access control mechanisms will ensure future grids are resilient, 
sustainable, and responsive to growing energy demands. This study emphasizes AI’s 
transformative role in addressing the challenges of the early grid, enhancing the 
capabilities of the present smart grid, and shaping a secure, efficient, and adaptive 
next-generation grid aligned with future needs.

Introduction
The electricity grid, often referred to simply as "the grid," is one of the most transfor­
mative innovations in human history. Since its inception, it has played a critical role in 
driving industrial progress, economic growth, and societal development. The grid serves 
as the backbone of modern energy systems, enabling the generation, transmission, and 
distribution of electricity to billions of people and industries worldwide. The origins of 
the electricity grid can be traced back to the late 19th and early twentieth centuries, with 
the advent of centralized power generation systems. Pioneers like Thomas Edison and 
Nikola Tesla introduced groundbreaking technologies—direct current (DC) and alter­
nating current (AC), respectively—that laid the foundation for modern power systems. 
Early grids were localized, limited in capacity, and primarily designed to supply power to 
small communities or industries [1–3].
With the rapid industrialization of the twentieth century, the grid evolved into a more 
interconnected and expansive network. The widespread adoption of AC transmission, 
championed by Tesla and George Westinghouse, allowed electricity to be transported 
over long distances with minimal losses, revolutionizing power delivery. This develop­
ment facilitated the construction of large-scale power plants, which supplied electricity 
to an ever-expanding population and industrial base [4]. Despite these advancements, 
the traditional grid faced limitations, including inefficiencies, vulnerability to outages, 
and challenges in integrating diverse energy sources. These issues became more pro­
nounced in the late twentieth century as global energy demands surged and concerns 
about environmental sustainability grew [5].
In response, the electricity grid underwent a paradigm shift, transitioning from a 
centralized, one-way power flow system to a decentralized, dynamic, and intelligent 
network—known as the "smart grid." This evolution, driven by technological advance­
ments in digitalization, automation, and renewable energy integration, has significantly 
enhanced grid efficiency, reliability, and adaptability [6, 7]. The journey of the electricity 
grid from its origins to its current state is a testament to human ingenuity and the con­
tinuous quest for progress. As we look toward the future, the grid is poised to undergo 
further transformation, leveraging innovations in artificial intelligence, energy stor­
age, and distributed energy resources. These advancements promise not only to meet 
the growing demands of a rapidly changing energy landscape but also to support global 
efforts toward sustainability and resilience [8,9].

the Greek word for amber, in 1600. He also introduced terms like “electric force” and

Foundations of modern electricity
In 1800, Alessandro Volta invented the battery, followed by Humphry Davy’s “arc lamp” 
in 1808. Hans Christian Oersted’s 1820 discovery of the link between electricity and 
magnetism enabled Michael Faraday and Joseph Henry to develop a primitive motor 
[13]. By 1831, Faraday’s electromagnetic induction experiments demonstrated that mov­
ing a wire through a magnetic field induces an electric current, earning him the title 
"Father of Electricity" and establishing the foundation for electric generators [www.eia.
gov/kids; www.powermag.com].
Advancements in dynamo technology
In 1832, Hippolyte Pixii developed the first basic dynamo, later enhanced by Antonio 
Pacinotti in 1860 to produce continuous DC [14]. Significant progress followed, includ­
ing the 1867 invention of the self-exciting dynamo-electric generator by Werner von Sie­
mens, Charles Wheatstone, and S.A. Varley. Zenobe Gramme further advanced power 
generation with a dynamo capable of producing steady-state DC for motors [www.
mentalfloss.com]. By 1877, arc lighting illuminated streets globally, and Charles F. Brush 
introduced a reliable dynamo design for large-scale electricity distribution [15, 16]. In 
1879, Thomas Edison revolutionized lighting with his practical incandescent lamp [12]. 
The first central power grid, established in 1882 on Pearl Street, New York City, initially 
served 85 customers with both DC and AC power. Over time, AC’s efficiency for higher 
voltage transmission marked a transformative period in electric power generation [1, 2]. 
Nikola Tesla, a Serbian-American engineer and physicist, revolutionized the alternating 
current (AC) electricity supply system. He filed 30 patents covering innovations like the 
AC dynamo, transformer, and polyphase motor, which formed the foundation for AC 
power distribution’s widespread adoption [3].
Electric power system – structured environment
The modern power grid consists of three main components: generation, transmission, 
and distribution, collectively known as a structured or regulated power system. Various 
energy sources are converted into electrical energy using different types of power plants, 
such as nuclear, hydroelectric, fossil fuel-based, and increasingly, renewable energy 
sources. High-voltage transmission lines transport electricity over long distances to sub­
stations, where it is then distributed at lower voltages to homes and businesses via distri­
bution lines [17].

Early electric power transmission systems
Electric power transmission refers to transferring electricity from generating stations 
to consumers via interconnected wires. Initially, transmission and distribution were not 
distinct, functioning seamlessly together. Before electricity, several transmission sys­
tems were developed, including telodynamic (cable in motion), pneumatic, and hydrau­
lic systems [4]. Telodynamic transmission, used in cable cars, enabled long-distance 
lines. Pneumatic systems powered local lighting in cities like Paris and others. Hydrau­
lic transmission, used in the late nineteenth century, supplied power to factory motors, 
such as in London, where a 290 km hydraulic network delivered 5.2 MW. These systems 
were cost-effective, but the power sector aimed to establish high-power transmission by 
the end of the nineteenth century [23].
The evolution of early power transmission
Early power transmission faced two key challenges: accommodating different voltages 
for various devices and placing generators near loads. These were addressed with volt­
age transformation, allowing power to be transmitted over a universal line [24]. Initially, 
direct current (DC) was used for lighting and industrial motors, but voltage adjustments 
were difficult, leading industries to install small generators near their needs [5]. The 
1879 invention of the incandescent light bulb prompted Edison to establish a large-scale 
electric company in Manhattan by 1882, powered by six 100 kW dynamos. Although 
it could power up to 1,200 lamps, the high costs led to the system’s demise by 1890. In

George Westinghouse identified inefficiencies in Edison’s low-voltage systems and 
promoted high-voltage alternating current (AC) for long-distance transmission, empha­
sizing cost-effective voltage conversion [4]. Transformers played a key role in AC’s supe­

1876 [25]. In 1881, Lucien Gaulard and John Dixen Gibbs improved transformer effi­
ciency with a more efficient step-down transformer [26].
Milestones in the evolution of long-distance AC power transmission
The first long-distance AC transmission line was built in 1884 for the International Exhi­
bition in Turin, Italy, covering 42 km with bronze wires supported by wooden poles and 
bell insulators. Around the same time, the U.S. adopted bronze and copper industrial 
power lines. Rome introduced the first operational AC line for public lighting in 1885, 
powered by two 22 kW alternators operating at 120 Hz. It utilized 200 series-connected 
step-down transformers, paving the way for modern transmission using economical 
transformers. In 1886, Westinghouse, William Stanley, and Franklin Pope refined this 
concept, with Westinghouse developing an AC motor for industrial use in 1888 [27]. The 
1891 International Electro-Technical Exhibition in Germany demonstrated high-power 
three-phase current, and by 1897, aluminum wires replaced copper and bronze. Early 
transmission lines used porcelain insulators that handled voltages up to 40 kV, but in 
1907, Harold W. Buck and Edward M. Hewlett introduced disc insulators for higher volt­
ages [28].
By the late twentieth century, transmission voltages had greatly advanced. In 1914, 
fifty-five systems operated above 70,000 V, and by 1919, Europe completed a 110 kV line 
between Lauchhammer and Riesa. In the 1920s, the U.S. built a 200 kV line from the 
Sierra Nevada to San Francisco, later upgraded to 380 kV. Germany established its first 
380 kV line in 1957. Hydro-Quebec introduced a 735 kV line in 1965, followed by the 
Soviet Union’s 1,200 kV line in 1982 [29].
The advancements of high-voltage DC (HVDC) transmission systems
The inefficiencies of conventional AC systems for long-distance transmission high­
lighted the need for Direct Current (DC) systems. AC systems were initially favored for 
their ease of voltage transformation and minimal losses over shorter distances. However, 
growing power demands and the need for efficient long-distance transmission revealed 
AC limitations, such as higher losses and synchronization challenges. Advances in high-
voltage direct current (HVDC) technology and power electronics renewed interest in 
DC transmission. HVDC enables efficient, stable electricity transmission over long dis­
tances and between asynchronous grids, particularly in underground and underwater 
applications where AC incurs significant losses. It also supports integrating renewable 
energy sources, including offshore wind farms [30]. The adoption of HVDC systems has 
driven power sector growth, becoming essential for emerging economies and fostering 
rural electrification, improved living standards, and economic growth [31].
While AC transmission remains versatile for shorter distances, HVDC systems 
increasingly dominate long-distance transmission. HVDC’s viability emerged with 
high-power AC-to-DC converters, first demonstrated by General Electric in 1936,

In a modern distribution system, high-voltage electricity from transmission lines is 
converted to low or medium voltage, typically between 2 and 33 kV, through step-down 
transformers. This system is divided into primary and secondary distribution. The pri­
mary distribution lines deliver medium voltage power to consumers via distribution 
transformers, which then reduce the voltage further to suit residential, industrial, and 
commercial applications [35]. Consumers with high-voltage needs may connect directly 
to the primary distribution or sub-transmission levels. Multiple steps occur at substa­
tions as power transitions from transmission to distribution [30, 31].
While regulated power systems provide stability, they present certain limitations. The 
lack of competitive pressure in monopolized utility sectors can stifle innovation and 
reduce efficiency improvements. Consequently, consumers often face limited choices, 
potentially higher costs, and limited customer service improvements due to the absence 
of competition. Additionally, the complex regulatory framework can slow decision-mak­
ing and rate-setting processes, potentially delaying investments and the adoption of new 
technologies. This framework can also hinder the rapid adoption of modern technologies 
and the integration of renewable energy sources [35]. Furthermore, regulatory capture 
and political influence may shape decisions, sometimes to the detriment of consumer 
welfare. Thus, regulated systems offer stability but can also hinder innovation, efficiency, 
and consumer choice compared to competitive market-based alternatives [33].

Deregulation and market reform
In the 1990s, electrical markets began to shift towards deregulation and liberalization. 
Many countries moved away from vertically integrated monopolies towards competi­
tive, deregulated markets. This transition involved unbundling the generation, transmis­
sion, and distribution functions to enhance efficiency, foster competition, and provide 
consumers with more choices. Key aspects of deregulated networks include separating 
generation and retail from transmission and distribution, enabling different suppliers to 
compete on price and service quality, and implementing market rules and safeguards to 
prevent manipulation and ensure reliability [4].
Evolution of smart grids
A deregulated power system enables multiple companies to generate, transmit, and sell 
electricity, fostering customer choice and competition. Unlike traditional regulated sys­
tems where a single utility oversees all aspects of supply, deregulation separates the gen­
eration and retail segments from transmission and distribution. This unbundling aims to 
lower costs and spur innovation by allowing customers to choose their electricity pro­
vider based on price and service quality. Deregulated markets encourage efficiency by 
promoting competitive pricing and incentivizing utilities to streamline operations and 
invest in new technologies. However, they also introduce complexities, such as price 
volatility and regulatory challenges, which require rigorous oversight to prevent market 
manipulation and ensure reliable service [6, 7].

[162]. These technologies enable better energy flow management, fault detection, and 
system performance optimization through the use of smart meters, sensors, and auto­

managing the variability of renewable energy sources. These systems will capture excess 
energy during periods of high generation and release it during peak demand or low gen­
eration times [166]. When paired with demand response programs that incentivize users

aid in stabilizing the grid and reduce the need for fossil fuel-dependent peaking power 
plants [19, 167].

dination to meet grid demands, lowering peak load stress, and boosting energy effi­

Enhancing cybersecurity and resilience in digitally integrated power grids
The smart grid, comprising sensors, displays, high-performance computing systems, and 
interconnected devices, plays a vital role in data collection, processing, and system con­
trol. However, its reliance on digital technologies creates significant cybersecurity vul­
nerabilities. The interconnected nature of smart grid components introduces multiple 
entry points for cyberattacks, increasing the risk of data breaches, system manipulation,

nuclear power station attack linked to a compromised network, the 2006 Alabama Ferry 
disruption due to network congestion, and the 2011 Stuxnet malware attack on Iran’s

The rising complexity of modern power grids, driven by increasing energy demands

as Role-Based Access Control (RBAC), which restricts unauthorized access to mitigate 
risks [178]. However, traditional RBAC models often fall short in addressing cross-
domain security challenges faced by interconnected modern grids [179, 180]. To over­
come these challenges, AI-driven security solutions can play a pivotal role by automating 
threat detection, predicting vulnerabilities, and dynamically adjusting access controls. 
These AI technologies enhance proactive risk management, improve real-time threat 
responses, and strengthen grid resilience in the face of evolving cyber threats [181].

advanced strategies like predictive maintenance, enabled by real-time analysis of oper­

approaches include machine learning-based resilience planning and the combination

grid systems through strategies such as transfer learning and AI integration. This con­

flexibility, and efficiency [130]. Addressing cybersecurity threats through these techno­

Conclusion
This comprehensive review delves into the evolution of the electrical grid, charting its 
journey from the early systems of generation, transmission, and distribution to the con­
temporary smart grid and its envisioned future. It underscores the historical milestones 
that have shaped the electric grid while highlighting the transformative influence of arti­
ficial intelligence (AI) in modernizing grid operations. AI has become a cornerstone in 
the development of smart grids, enabling capabilities such as advanced decision-mak­
ing, predictive analytics, real-time monitoring, automated management, and enhanced 
cybersecurity. These innovations effectively address traditional grid limitations, includ­
ing inefficiencies, vulnerabilities, and challenges in integrating renewable energy sources, 
electric vehicles, and energy storage systems. The review also explores the emerging 
technologies poised to redefine the future grid, including Digital Twin (DT) models, the 
Internet of Energy (IoE), and decentralized energy management systems. These tech­
nologies offer advanced solutions such as real-time simulations, adaptive control mech­
anisms, and improved human–machine interaction, paving the way for proactive risk 
management and efficient energy distribution. However, the study also highlights the 
challenges associated with these innovations, particularly in addressing cybersecurity 
threats and ensuring robust implementation. In addition, the role of the future electric 
grid in achieving the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) is dis­
cussed, emphasizing its contribution to resilience, sustainability, and adaptability. This

Abstract: The evolution of the electrical grid from its early centralized structure to today’s advanced “smart grid” reflects significant technological progress. Early grids, designed for simple power delivery from large plants to consumers, faced challenges in efficiency, reliability, and scalability. Over time, the grid has transformed into a decentralized network driven by innovative technologies, particularly artificial intelligence (AI). AI has become instrumental in enhancing efficiency, security, and resilience by enabling real-time data analysis, predictive maintenance, demand- response optimization, and automated fault detection, thereby improving overall operational efficiency. This paper examines the evolution of the electrical grid, tracing its transition from early limitations to the methodologies adopted in present smart grids for addressing those challenges. Current smart grids leverage AI to optimize energy management, predict faults, and seamlessly integrate electric vehicles (EVs), reducing transmission losses and improving performance. However, these advancements are not without limitations. Present grids remain vulnerable to cyberattacks, necessitating the adoption of more robust methodologies and advanced technologies for future grids. Looking forward, emerging technologies such as Digital Twin (DT) models, the Internet of Energy (IoE), and decentralized grid management are set to redefine grid architectures. These advanced technologies enable real-time simulations, adaptive control, and enhanced human–machine collaboration, supporting dynamic energy distribution and proactive risk management. Integrating AI with advanced energy storage, renewable resources, and adaptive access control mechanisms will ensure future grids are resilient, sustainable, and responsive to growing energy demands. This study emphasizes AI’s transformative role in addressing the challenges of the early grid, enhancing the capabilities of the present smart grid, and shaping a secure, efficient, and adaptive next-generation grid aligned with future needs.
